R5:physical.title: Turbulent fluid flow (direct numerical simulation)
R5:physical.summary: Compute-bound in the framer's strict sense. The Navier-Stokes equations are trusted, and DNS cost grows as Re^3, so compute buys resolution that removes turbulence-closure error. Contact and cloth have no tractable trusted fine-scale equation to resolve in the same way.

R5:physical.title: Learned weather emulators (GraphCast)
R5:physical.summary: Trained on four decades of ERA5 reanalysis, it beats operational systems on 90% of 1,380 targets and forecasts in under a minute on one TPU v4. It shows a learned simulator becoming compute-bound because a trusted corpus already existed. Robotics has no equivalent corpus for contact.

roots.question: Can scientific paper reviews (maybe specifically ML, DL, data-driven papers) be automated with highly scoped, small subagents following the AISLE model: many open-source models, since they have different blind spots, with tasks scoped to known failure modes like biases, factual reproduction errors, 'do these authors/papers exist' errors and overclaims, including building the suggested experiments and variations and running them on GPUs? Is compute a major blocker at some level, could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it?

What's actually stopping general purpose robot hands from reliably doing stuff like folding laundry or loading a dishwasher? Is it the lack of real-world manipulation data, the hardware (sensors, actuators, tactile feedback), or the sim-to-real gap? Is that a major blocker at some level, and could it be fixed by running millions of simulated robots in parallel on a shit ton of GPUs?

Why can't we predict earthquakes days or hours in advance? Is it fundamentally chaotic physics that no model can get around, or is it mostly a data problem with too few sensors and too few big quakes to learn from? Could training huge foundation models on decades of global seismic waveforms, GPS strain and fault simulations with a shit ton of GPU parallelism actually get somewhere, or is compute not the blocker at all?

What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one?

What limits general-purpose robot manipulation right now? Is it lack of real-world data, the sim-to-real gap, or hardware like hands and tactile sensors? If you can already run millions of simulated environments in parallel on GPUs with heavy domain randomization, why can't you brute-force a policy that folds laundry or ties knots and then transfers to a real robot? Is contact and deformable-object physics the wall that no amount of compute gets you over because the simulator itself is wrong in ways you can't randomize away? Or could a shit ton of GPU parallelism plus a small fleet of real robots that keeps correcting the simulator close the loop?

plan.question: On one rented GPU node, does the cost of direct simulation grow as Reynolds number to the sixth power, and does finer resolution remove the error a turbulence model leaves?
plan.hypothesis: Compute buys fidelity for small-scale statistics that closures discard, while cheap closures stay cheaper for large-scale quantities at modest Reynolds number.

compute_axis.quantity: Grid points per side N: at fixed viscosity (Q2) and with Reynolds number rising at fixed k_max*eta (Q1)

held_fixed: JHTDB 1024^3 viscosity 0.000185 in the fixed-physics ladder (Q2)
Forcing: hold total energy in modes |k|<=2 constant
Time scheme: integrating factor plus second-order Adams-Bashforth
k_max*eta about 1.35 in the Reynolds ladder (Q1)

predictions.if_lever: Fully resolved simulation matches the published 1024^3 statistics within tolerance. Unmodeled simulation error in velocity-gradient statistics falls as grid size N grows, while large-eddy simulation keeps an error floor.
predictions.if_not: Smagorinsky LES matches gradient statistics at equal cost, or resolved DNS misses the published statistics, so extra resolution does not remove closure error.
predictions.decision_rule: Reproduction passes if Re_lambda is within 4% of 418, E_tot within 3% of 0.705 and epsilon within 10% of 0.103. Lever holds if no-model DNS error in gradient skewness and flatness falls with N while LES at every tested constant keeps an error floor.
predictions.noise_rule: Pass limits come from variability in the published time series (Re_lambda SD 10.8; epsilon moves about 10% between 1 T_L and 5 T_L averaging). Average over at least 10 T_L; widen spectrum tolerance to 3x own block-to-block standard error if larger.
predictions.expected_why: The file predicts compute buys fidelity for gradient quantities the closure throws away, while LES stays cheaper for large-scale quantities.

plan.compute_tested_why: Grid size N, which more GPUs and memory buy, is raised from 128 to 1024 (2048 gated), and cost per turnover is measured against it.
plan.scored_against: JHTDB 1024^3 published statistics (README values, spectrum.txt, time series), plus Taylor-Green Re=1600 reference dissipation and exact-solution tests.

anchor.what: Reproduce the published 1024^3 forced isotropic run: Taylor-scale Reynolds number 418, averaged over at least 10 turnover times [jhtdb_readme]
anchor.tolerance: Re_lambda within 4%; E_tot within 3% of 0.705; epsilon within 10% of 0.103; u', lambda, eta, L, T_L within 5%; E(k) within 10% for 3<=k<=400

checks: Tier 1: exact 2-D Taylor-Green decay relative L2 error <= 1e-12 in fp64, at P=1 and P=8
Halving dt three times gives error ratio approaching 4 (second order)
Unforced -dE/dt equals 2*nu*enstrophy; forced injected power balances epsilon; pass at <=0.1% at 128^3
P=1 versus P=8 relative L2 difference <= 1e-10 after 200 steps at 256^3
Tier 2: Taylor-Green Re=1600 peak dissipation within 2.5% at 256^3 and 1% at 512^3
Tier 3: JHTDB reproduction criteria; own 2*nu*sum k^2 E(k) matches injected power within 2%
Tier 4: C_eps and velocity-derivative skewness change smoothly with Re_lambda and meet JHTDB value at 1024^3
Optional pointwise comparison against JHTDB fine dataset if it continues from the t=0 frame

Benchmark 1024^3 for 1 h each on 1x B200 and 8x H100; optionally 512^3 on 1x GH200

plan.option_title: Medium-range weather forecasting with learned models
plan.question: At 1.5 degrees on a $1,000 budget, does GraphCast-style forecast skill improve more from 4 times the training compute or from 4 times the years of reanalysis data?
plan.hypothesis: Quadrupling compute at 40 years improves day-5 Z500 RMSE more than quadrupling data from 10 to 40 years, because the 40-year record is near saturation [arXiv 2212.12794].

compute_axis.quantity: training compute per run as a fraction of T (about 21 GPU-hours on one H100), at 40 years of data

held_fixed: Architecture: GraphCast_small processor (config A, latent 512) or config B (latent 256) chosen once by pilot throughput
Optimizer: AdamW, betas 0.9/0.95, weight decay 0.1, clip 32, 1,000-step warmup to 1e-3, half-cosine decay
Normalization statistics: DeepMind's published files, same for every run
Evaluation: WB2 evaluate.py on 732 forecasts in 2020
Last 10% of each run's wall-clock on 2 to 4 rollout steps

predictions.if_lever: The day-5 Z500 RMSE gain from 4x compute at 40 years exceeds the gain from 4x data at full compute by more than twice the seed noise.
predictions.if_not: D exceeds C by more than twice the seed noise (data-bound), or neither exceeds the other by that margin (inconclusive).
predictions.decision_rule: C = RMSE(40y, T/4) - RMSE(40y, T); D = RMSE(10y recent, T) - RMSE(40y, T). C > D + 2N: compute-bound. D > C + 2N: data-bound. Otherwise inconclusive.
predictions.noise_rule: N = |seed 0 - seed 1| per metric and lead time from the two 40-year runs. Effects smaller than 2N are reported as null. Paired per-forecast differences with a one-week block bootstrap.
predictions.expected_why: The file predicts that 4x compute at 40 years beats 4x data, since GraphCast's authors found older data of little benefit.

plan.compute_tested_why: Runs at T/4, T/2 and T on the same 40-year data directly vary training compute, which more parallel GPUs buy.

records.card: **W5 · Learned weather emulators (GraphCast).** R5 · physical · random pick · compute tested: yes · plan expects: the lever · halted: cost record broken **Question.** At 1.5 degrees on a $1,000 budget, does GraphCast-style forecast skill improve more from 4 times the training compute or from 4 times the years of reanalysis data? **What is known.** GraphCast's authors found adding 1959-1978 data had little benefit, and ArchesWeather found older ERA5 harder to fit; neither varied years of data against compute under one setup [arXiv 2212.12794, 2405.14527]. A matched comparison of years of reanalysis versus training compute, same architecture and evaluation, at 1.5 degrees. The file found none, but its web search was exhausted. **Hypothesis.** Quadrupling compute at 40 years improves day-5 Z500 RMSE more than quadrupling data from 10 to 40 years, because the 40-year record is near saturation [arXiv 2212.12794]. **If compute is the lever.** The day-5 Z500 RMSE gain from 4x compute at 40 years exceeds the gain from 4x data at full compute by more than twice the seed noise. **If not.** D exceeds C by more than twice the seed noise (data-bound), or neither exceeds the other by that margin (inconclusive). **Test.** Train ten GraphCast-style models at 1.5 degrees on one 8x H100 machine, varying years of ERA5 data (5 to 40) and compute (1/4 to 1x). Compare day-5 Z500 error gains from compute and data against seed noise and WB2 baselines. *Compute axis.* Training compute per run as a fraction of T (about 21 GPU-hours on one H100), at 40 years of data: 0.25–1 fraction of T, 3 levels. Closest prior: not on this axis. Prior art checked without web search. *Restructuring.* none. **Check first.** Our evaluation code run on WB2's stored 2020 forecasts reproduces published scores: GraphCast T2M day 5 = 1.252, HRES T2M = 1.334, HRES Z500 = 304.35. Tolerance: within 0.5% (design threshold). **Would not show.** Single resolution (1.5 degrees) and one architecture family. Fixed small budget; day-10 RMSE differences may reflect blur, not skill. Only two seeds, at one configuration; a 2025-2026 reproduction may exist unfound. *Cost.* Plans $834.46 of the $1,000 budget over 39 machine-hours, leaving $165.54.
